newsitem.title: INDIA: India state asks for troops to combat tribals.
newsitem.headline: India state asks for troops to combat tribals.

text.p: India began gearing up on Thursday for a security clampdown to combat tribal insurgents in the troubled northeast state of Assam after a train bomb that killed dozens of people earlier this week.
The state government has asked New Delhi to send 130 paramilitary companies, or about 26,000 men, almost doubling the force already in Assam, officials said.
K. Padmanabhaiah, the highest ranking civil servant in the federal Home (Interior) Ministry, flew to the state's main city Guwahati on Thursday for emergency talks with Assam officials.
"Padmanabhaiah will meet senior police, civil and military officials to discuss the security level in the state," a senior police officer in Guwahati told Reuters.

The ruling party in Assam is a member of Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's fragile coalition, strengthening the likelihood the state will receive the additional security forces, authorities said.

Assam chief minister Prafulla Kumar Mahanta, leader of the regional Assam Gana Parishad party, convened an all party meeting to discuss the worsening violence in the state, and called on Bodo tribal militants to seek a negotiated settlement.
Bodo tribals, living in northwest Assam between the north bank of the Brahmaputra river and the foothills of the Himalayas, are fighting for a homeland that would split the state in two.

The train attack was the biggest blow so far in a concerted campaign that appears to have been stepped up since Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda came to Guwahati in October offering money but no hope of independence.
The central government has budgeted six billion rupees ($170 million) for the development of seven impoverished states in the remote northeast, including the largest, Assam.
Bodos account for about 800,000 of Assam's 25 million people. Over the past two decades, swarms of immigrants from Bangladesh and Santhals, a tribe from Bihar, have settled in their tribal lands.
Bodos, who mainly live in forests, have objected to extensive logging that has devastated the environment and upset the tribe's traditional way of life.
Since 1987, Bodos have been fighting immigrants, security forces and, at times, themselves. Police say some 5,000 people have been killed in insurgency-related violence.

Police in Kokrajhar, the main town and district where Monday's train attack took place, began a sweep of rural villages that are a breeding ground for militants belonging to the Bodoland Liberation Tigers Force (BLTF).

The BLTF is the prime suspect for the explosion, which wrecked the Brahmaputra Mail passenger train, killing 33 people according to the official death toll. Some local authorities who asked not to be named have said the toll was higher.
Railway traffic between northeastern India and the rest of the nation, severed in the attack, was restored on Thursday, the Press Trust of India said.
Factional fighting between the BLTF and rival Bodoland Army militants, formerly called the Bodo Security Force, had produced most of the recent violence until Monday's train blast.

BLTF extremists are believed to be supporters of activists in the All Bodo Students Union (ABSU) movement. The Bodoland Army is linked to ABSU's bitter rival, the People's Democratic Front, a party with a handful of seats in the state assembly.
The Bodoland Army is the larger and more disciplined of the two guerrilla groups. Assam security sources believe it has 16 camps in the Himalayan foothills inside neighbouring Bhutan.
